title: Weimar Germany & the Rise of the Nazis
description: How Germany went from defeat in 1918 through the crises and recovery of the Weimar Republic to Hitler becoming Chancellor in 1933.

notes.heading: Germany in 1918: Defeat and a New Republic
notes.body: By autumn 1918 Germany was losing the First World War. Its allies had collapsed, the British blockade had left civilians short of food, and the army was retreating. In November 1918 sailors at Kiel mutinied, strikes and protests spread across the country, and Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated. On 11 November 1918 the new German government signed the armistice that ended the fighting. Many Germans felt betrayed — the army had never been defeated on German soil, so a myth grew up that Germany had been 'stabbed in the back' by politicians at home. The politicians who signed the armistice were later nicknamed the 'November Criminals'. A new democratic system, the Weimar Republic, was set up in 1919. It had an elected parliament (the Reichstag) chosen by proportional representation, and a president with strong emergency powers. Its weaknesses — too many small parties, frequent coalition governments, and widespread hatred of it from the start — would matter enormously later.

notes.heading: The Treaty of Versailles and Its Impact
notes.body: In June 1919 the victorious Allies forced Germany to sign the Treaty of Versailles. Its main terms can be remembered as BRAT: Blame (Article 231, the 'war guilt clause', said Germany was responsible for the war), Reparations (Germany had to pay huge sums to the Allies, eventually fixed at £6.6 billion), Army (the German army was limited to 100,000 men, with no tanks, aircraft or submarines, and the Rhineland was demilitarised), and Territory (Germany lost about 13% of its land, including Alsace-Lorraine to France and all of its overseas colonies). Germans were outraged: they called it a 'Diktat' — a dictated peace they had no say in. The treaty mattered for two reasons. First, it caused real economic and political pain. Second, and perhaps more importantly, it gave extremists a permanent grievance — politicians like Hitler could blame every problem on Versailles and the 'November Criminals' who had accepted it.

notes.heading: The Crisis Year of 1923: Hyperinflation and the Munich Putsch
notes.body: In 1923 the Weimar Republic nearly collapsed. When Germany fell behind on reparations, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr, Germany's main industrial region. German workers went on strike, and the government paid them by simply printing more money. With more money chasing fewer goods, prices exploded — this is hyperinflation. A loaf of bread that cost about 250 marks in January 1923 cost around 200 billion marks by November. Savings and pensions became worthless overnight, though people with debts or mortgages actually benefited. In the chaos, a small extremist group in Munich tried to seize power. In November 1923 Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party attempted the Munich Putsch, an armed uprising that was quickly crushed by police. Hitler was sent to prison, where he wrote Mein Kampf and learned a crucial lesson: the Nazis would win power through elections, not violence. In late 1923 a new currency, the Rentenmark, stabilised the economy — but ordinary Germans never forgot the terror of hyperinflation.

notes.heading: The 'Golden Twenties' under Stresemann
notes.body: From 1924 to 1929 Gustav Stresemann, as foreign minister and briefly chancellor, led Germany's recovery — a period sometimes called the 'Golden Twenties'. The Dawes Plan (1924) reorganised reparation payments and brought in huge American loans, which restarted German industry. The Locarno Pact (1925) saw Germany accept its western borders, improving relations with France and Britain. Germany joined the League of Nations in 1926, and the Young Plan (1929) reduced reparations further. At home, the economy grew and cities like Berlin became famous for exciting art, cinema and cabaret. However, the recovery was fragile. It depended on American loans that could be withdrawn at any time. Farmers were struggling with falling prices, and many older, traditional Germans disliked the new culture. Meanwhile the Nazi Party used these quieter years to reorganise itself into a modern, disciplined national party — ready to take advantage of the next crisis.

notes.heading: The Wall Street Crash and the Depression
notes.body: In October 1929 share prices on the New York Stock Exchange collapsed — the Wall Street Crash. American banks and businesses immediately demanded the return of the loans they had poured into Germany. The result was the Great Depression in Germany: factories closed, banks failed and unemployment soared from about 1.3 million in 1929 to over 6 million by 1932 — roughly one in three workers. Millions more were on short hours or reduced pay. People lost their homes, queued at soup kitchens, and lost faith in the democratic politicians who seemed unable to help. The Weimar system made things worse: coalition governments argued about how to respond and kept collapsing, so from 1930 the president increasingly ruled by emergency decree instead of through the Reichstag. This taught Germans to see democracy itself as weak and divided. Extremist parties offering simple, radical answers — the Communists on the left and the Nazis on the right — gained support at the expense of moderate parties.

notes.heading: Nazi Ideology and Tactics
notes.body: The Nazi Party offered a clear, aggressive ideology. Its key ideas were: overturning the Treaty of Versailles; extreme nationalism and a strong Germany; racial theories that falsely claimed Germans were a 'master race' and viciously blamed Jewish people for Germany's problems (antisemitism); Lebensraum ('living space') — expansion eastwards; and the destruction of communism. Hitler himself was a powerful, hypnotic speaker. The party's tactics were modern and ruthless. Joseph Goebbels ran sophisticated propaganda: mass rallies, posters, radio and films hammered home simple slogans, and the Nazis used new technology — Hitler even flew between rallies by aeroplane. The SA (the 'Brownshirts') were the party's street army, beating up opponents and breaking up rival meetings, which made the Nazis look strong and made politics violent. Different messages were aimed at different groups: jobs for the unemployed, order for the middle classes, protection from communism for businessmen. Crucially, the Nazis posed as the only force that could save Germany from a Communist revolution — which frightened many wealthy and middle-class Germans into supporting them.

notes.heading: From Votes to Power: Hitler Becomes Chancellor
notes.body: The Depression turned the Nazis from a fringe party into a mass movement. In 1928 they had won just 12 seats in the Reichstag; by July 1932 they were the largest party with 230 seats — though never a majority, and they actually lost seats in November 1932. So why did Hitler become Chancellor on 30 January 1933? Not through a majority vote, but through a back-room deal. Conservative politicians around the elderly President Hindenburg — especially Franz von Papen — believed they could use Hitler's popularity and control him, famously underestimating him. Hindenburg reluctantly appointed Hitler Chancellor of a coalition government in which only three ministers were Nazis. The reasons for Nazi success can be summed up: the Depression created despair; Nazi propaganda and organisation were superb; Hitler's speeches inspired many; the SA spread fear; fear of communism pushed the rich towards Hitler; Weimar democracy was weak and discredited; and conservative elites made the fatal mistake of thinking they could tame him. Within months, those elites discovered how wrong they had been.

flashcards.definition: Germany's democratic government from 1919 to 1933, with an elected Reichstag (parliament) and a president. Weakened by proportional representation, coalition governments and hatred of the Versailles settlement.
flashcards.example: Named after the town of Weimar, where the new constitution was agreed in 1919.

flashcards.definition: The 1919 peace treaty ending the First World War. Its terms (BRAT): war Blame, Reparations of £6.6 billion, Army limited to 100,000 men, and Territory losses of about 13% of German land.
flashcards.example: Germans called it a 'Diktat' — a dictated peace they had no part in negotiating.

flashcards.definition: The collapse in value of the German mark in 1923, caused partly by the government printing money during the Ruhr occupation. Prices rose billions of times; savings and pensions became worthless.
flashcards.example: A loaf of bread costing 250 marks in January 1923 cost about 200 billion marks by November.

flashcards.definition: The Nazis' failed attempt to seize power by force in Munich in November 1923. Hitler was imprisoned and wrote Mein Kampf, deciding to win power legally through elections instead.
flashcards.example: The putsch taught Hitler that armed revolt would fail against the army and police.

flashcards.definition: German foreign minister (1923–29) who led the recovery of the 'Golden Twenties': the Dawes Plan, Locarno Pact and joining the League of Nations.
flashcards.example: He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1926 for improving relations with France.

flashcards.definition: An American-backed plan that reorganised German reparation payments and provided large US loans, restarting German industry — but making Germany dependent on American money.
flashcards.example: When American loans were recalled after 1929, the German economy collapsed.

flashcards.definition: The collapse of share prices on the New York Stock Exchange in October 1929, which triggered the worldwide Great Depression as American loans to Germany were withdrawn.
flashcards.example: German unemployment rose from 1.3 million in 1929 to over 6 million by 1932.

flashcards.definition: The economic crisis after 1929: mass unemployment, bank failures and poverty, which destroyed faith in Weimar democracy and drove voters towards extremist parties.
flashcards.example: By 1932 about one in three German workers was unemployed.

flashcards.definition: The Nazi Party's paramilitary street army, led by Ernst Röhm, which attacked opponents, broke up rival meetings and made the Nazis appear strong and orderly.
flashcards.example: SA violence intimidated voters and made Communist meetings almost impossible.

flashcards.definition: The Nazi propaganda chief who used rallies, posters, radio, film and simple repeated slogans to build support, tailoring messages to different groups of voters.
flashcards.example: He organised Hitler's aeroplane tours so the leader could speak in several cities a day.

flashcards.definition: Meaning 'living space': the Nazi goal of expanding Germany eastwards into lands such as Poland and the Soviet Union to gain territory and resources.
flashcards.example: This aim was set out by Hitler in Mein Kampf in the 1920s.

flashcards.definition: The head of the German government, roughly equivalent to a prime minister. Hitler was appointed Chancellor by President Hindenburg on 30 January 1933 as part of a coalition deal.
flashcards.example: Conservative politicians backed the appointment believing they could control Hitler.

questions.stem: In which year was the Treaty of Versailles signed?
questions.explanation: The Treaty of Versailles was signed in June 1919, after the armistice of November 1918 had ended the fighting in the First World War.

questions.stem: What does the 'R' in BRAT (the terms of the Treaty of Versailles) stand for?
choices: Retreat
Revolution
Reparations
Rationing
questions.explanation: BRAT stands for Blame, Reparations, Army and Territory. Reparations were the payments Germany had to make to the Allies, eventually fixed at £6.6 billion.

questions.stem: Who benefited from the hyperinflation of 1923?
choices: Pensioners living on fixed incomes
People with large savings in the bank
People with debts and mortgages
Foreign tourists visiting Germany
questions.explanation: Because money became almost worthless, debts could be paid off with worthless notes, so borrowers benefited. Savers and pensioners on fixed incomes were the big losers.

questions.stem: What was the most important lesson Hitler learned from the failure of the Munich Putsch?
choices: That the Nazi Party should give up on winning power
That he needed support from the Soviet Union
That propaganda was useless
That the Nazis should win power through elections rather than armed revolt
questions.explanation: The failed putsch of 1923 showed Hitler that force would be crushed by the army and police. In prison he decided the Nazis would instead campaign for votes and seize power legally.

questions.stem: Which agreement of 1924 reorganised reparations and brought American loans into Germany?
choices: The Dawes Plan
The Young Plan
The Locarno Pact
The Treaty of Versailles
questions.explanation: The Dawes Plan (1924) rescheduled reparation payments and opened the door to huge American loans. The Young Plan (1929) came later and reduced the total amount owed.

questions.stem: Why was the prosperity of the 'Golden Twenties' described as fragile?
choices: It was based only on farming
It depended on American loans that could be withdrawn at any time
Most Germans refused to work in factories
The Reichstag banned new businesses
questions.explanation: German recovery rested on short-term American loans. When the Wall Street Crash hit in 1929, those loans were recalled and the German economy collapsed almost immediately.

questions.stem: By 1932, roughly how many Germans were unemployed?
choices: About 100,000
About 500,000
About 1 million
Over 6 million
questions.explanation: Unemployment rose from 1.3 million in 1929 to over 6 million by 1932 — about one in three workers, with millions more on short time.

questions.stem: Which factor best explains why wealthy businessmen and many middle-class Germans supported the Nazis after 1929?
choices: The Nazis promised to nationalise all big businesses
Fear of a Communist revolution pushed them towards Hitler, who posed as Germany's saviour from communism
The Nazis promised to cut wages for workers
They wanted Germany to return to rule by the Kaiser
questions.explanation: As Communist support grew in the Depression, businessmen and the middle classes feared a revolution like Russia's in 1917. Hitler presented himself as the strongman who would destroy communism, so they funded and backed him.

questions.stem: Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933. How did this happen?
choices: The Nazis won a majority of seats in the Reichstag and claimed power
The SA seized control of Berlin in an armed coup
President Hindenburg appointed him after conservative politicians, led by von Papen, persuaded him they could control Hitler
The Allied powers ordered Germany to appoint him
questions.explanation: The Nazis never won a Reichstag majority. Hitler came to power through a back-room deal: von Papen and other conservatives convinced Hindenburg to appoint him, arrogantly believing they could tame him.

questions.stem: What was the 'stab in the back' myth?
choices: The false claim that Germany lost the First World War because politicians at home betrayed the unbeaten army
The attack on Hitler during the Munich Putsch
The assassination of the German president in 1919
The French invasion of the Ruhr in 1923
questions.explanation: Because no foreign army had invaded Germany, nationalists spread the false idea that the army had been betrayed by the 'November Criminals' who signed the armistice. Extremists used this myth to discredit democracy.

questions.stem: Who ran Nazi propaganda in the early 1930s?
choices: Ernst Röhm
Gustav Stresemann
Joseph Goebbels
Franz von Papen
questions.explanation: Joseph Goebbels organised the Nazis' modern propaganda machine — rallies, posters, radio and film — with simple slogans tailored to different audiences. Röhm led the SA; Stresemann was a Weimar statesman.

questions.stem: Which sequence of events is in the correct chronological order?
choices: Munich Putsch → hyperinflation → Wall Street Crash → Dawes Plan
Treaty of Versailles → hyperinflation and Munich Putsch → Dawes Plan → Wall Street Crash
Wall Street Crash → Treaty of Versailles → Dawes Plan → Munich Putsch
Dawes Plan → Munich Putsch → Wall Street Crash → Treaty of Versailles
questions.explanation: Versailles was 1919; hyperinflation and the Munich Putsch both came in the crisis year 1923; the Dawes Plan followed in 1924; the Wall Street Crash came in October 1929.

questions.stem: How did the Weimar constitution itself help undermine German democracy after 1930?
choices: It banned all political parties except one
Proportional representation produced weak coalitions, and the president could rule by emergency decree, bypassing the Reichstag
It gave the army control of the government
It forced Germany to hold elections every month
questions.explanation: Proportional representation meant no single party usually had a majority, so fragile coalitions kept collapsing during the Depression. From 1930 the president governed by emergency decree, teaching Germans to see parliament as pointless.

choices: The German parliament
The Nazi Party's paramilitary street army, known as the Brownshirts
A Jewish resistance organisation
The government agency that printed money in 1923
questions.explanation: The SA (Sturmabteilung), led by Ernst Röhm, was the Nazi street army. Its brown-uniformed members beat up opponents and broke up rival meetings, spreading fear while making the Nazis look powerful.

questions.stem: A historian argues: 'Without the Depression, Hitler would never have become Chancellor.' Which piece of evidence best supports this view?
choices: The Nazis won 12 seats in 1928 but became the largest party by July 1932, after unemployment passed 6 million
Hitler wrote Mein Kampf while in prison in 1924
The Treaty of Versailles limited the German army to 100,000 men
Stresemann won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1926
questions.explanation: The Nazi vote collapsed in the prosperous years (12 seats in 1928) and exploded during the Depression (230 seats in July 1932), showing that economic despair, not ideology alone, drove voters to Hitler.
